Released Oct 18, 2011 • 25th Anniversary of "Ignition (The Forger's Call)" • 80s Cosmic Pop

Released on Tuesday, October 18, 2011—twenty-five years to the exact day after "Ignition (The Forger's Call)" first detonated inside The Crucible on Homecoming Saturday, October 18, 1986—Starfield Calibration is the band's silver-anniversary gift to Forger Nation while recharging from their exhausting 2004 post-Progress Street burnout.

Rather than rushing back onto a high-friction stadium tour before Ryan and Cassidy were ready, Chief Audio Architect Cassidy O'Connell retreated to the family's private Blacksburg studio to rebuild fourteen foundational tracks (1987–2001) entirely within The Cosmic Tidal Lock Sound™—including retrospective lyric updates celebrating their liberation from Apex Records' "Plastic Sky" and the first-ever finalized studio master of "Atmosphere" (rescuing the song from its rough 1992 early-90s Friction demo and bringing it back to the lush 1980s sound the band loves so much).

While the Band Recharges, Holly Builds an Empire (1997 → 2011 → 2015)

To the outside world, the 2004–2014 Burnout Hiatus looked like a quiet retreat. Behind closed doors, CEO Holly O'Connell was executing an 18-year institutional wealth and liability blueprint she first conceived in 1997 during Hard Reset—when the "$13.99 War" and the 1996 "American Dream" Jackpot taught her that the family's capital and master catalog had to be ruthlessly siloed and diversified.

By the time Starfield Calibration dropped in October 2011, Holly had already stripped all operational liabilities out of Engine Room Records, LLC (2005), spun off Artists First Management, LLC and Stardust Strategic Assets, LLC (2005), built CPI barrier-free housing via Stardust Blacksburg, LLC (2007), and used the 2008–2010 financial crash to acquire Class-A Century City office towers for cash through Pacific Rim Properties, LLC (2009–2011)—laying the final bricks for The O'Connell Family Revocable Trust (2012) and the August 2015 Delaware Migration ($2.4B+ AUM).

html:
The Band

A Family Unit. A Creative Fortress.

To understand The Stardust Engine, you must first understand that they are not a "band" in the traditional sense; they are a true family. The O'Connell members (Ryan, Cassidy, and Holly) are siblings, and the Wright members (Evan and Tyler) are their identical twin cousins.

Their name came directly from the very first song the four of them wrote together in 1986 when Evan and Tyler joined Cassidy and Ryan at CPI: "The Stardust Engine". Too scared at the time to shop the song around, they kept it to themselves and decided to use that song to name their band—a tribute to their shared love of the cosmos ("Stardust") and the rockets to get you there ("Engine"). When the song was finally released a year later on 1987's Electric Color, Apex Records buried it at Track 13 and screwed around with the band's name—branding Cassidy as their "Stardust" and Ryan as their "Engine" in a cheap 1980s corporate marketing gimmick that the band despised because it took away from their love of the cosmos and the rockets to get you there.

Their close-knit bond is their defining feature. They are famously affectionate, often found piled on a single motel bed (the O'Connells on one, the Wrights on the other) or cuddling on a tour bus sofa. This family bond was their "Fortress" against an industry that tried to tear them apart.

The Family Unit (1997): Evan Wright, Cassidy O'Connell, Ryan O'Connell, Holly O'Connell, and Tyler Wright inside The Fortress.

title: Cassidy O'Connell | The Stardust Engine
description: Lead Vocals, Piano, Synthesizers
html:
Cassidy O'Connell

Lead Vocals, Piano, Synthesizers

  1. The Band
  2. Cassidy O'Connell

The "Anchor". Cassidy (Age 21 in 1987) is the emotional center of the band. Classically trained on piano, she brings the cinematic, orchestral texture that defines the band's "Space Rock" sound.

While Ryan provides the raw energy (The Engine), Cassidy provides the gravity. Her relationship with her brother is the core dynamic of the group; she is his "Safe Person," and he is hers. Their vocal harmonies—often described as "telepathic"—are the result of a lifetime of non-verbal communication.

The "Friction" Survivor

In 1992, Cassidy was the primary target of the "Friction" scandal. When Apex executives attempted to exploit her bond with Ryan for a marketing campaign, she didn't crumble—she went silent.

She famously refused to speak to *any* press for three years (1992-1995), communicating only through her lyrics on *The Warehouse Tapes*. Songs like "The Cage" and "Ad Astra" are her direct response to the trauma: a declaration that she would rather flee to the stars than sell her soul on Earth.

CONFIDENTIAL: The "American Dream" (1996)

The Daleville Event

In 1996, four years after the band declared independence, they were driving home from a gig in Lexington, VA. They stopped at a gas station in Daleville for late-night snacks and fuel. On a whim, Cassidy bought a "Quick Pick" ticket for the American Dream lottery. She let the machine pick the numbers, simply liking the visual pattern they made on the screen.

The next morning, while reading the newspaper, it slowly dawned on her: she had matched all numbers in correct order, including the Dream Ball.

She didn't scream. She walked into the kitchen, handed the ticket to her sister Holly, and said, "Build us a fortress so we never have to be hurt again." The jackpot was $2.04 Billion.

title: Evan Wright | The Stardust Engine
description: Bass Guitar, Rhythm Guitar, Backing Vocals
html:
Evan Wright

Bass Guitar, Rhythm Guitar, Backing Vocals

  1. The Band
  2. Evan Wright

The "Texture" of the band, Evan (Age 20 in 1987) is the secret weapon that makes their sound so full. He and his identical twin brother, Tyler Wright, are cousins to the O'Connell siblings. Together, the five of them form the tight-knit family unit that defines the group.

Evan is the quiet, steady presence in the "engine room," providing the rich, melodic basslines and atmospheric rhythm guitar that form the foundation for Ryan's solos. His bond with his twin brother is legendary; on tour during the Apex era, the twins were inseparable, famously taking one of the two cramped motel beds while the three O'Connell siblings piled into the other.

The Crash of '90: "The Human Ramp"

After his cousin Ryan's injury in 1990, the reality of touring changed instantly. While Holly and Cassidy handled the private medical logistics, it was Evan and Tyler who handled the brute force required to navigate a world built without ramps.

In 1991, venues rarely had elevators. If the band had to play a second-floor club, or if the "accessible ramp" was a dangerous piece of plywood, Evan and Tyler became the "Human Ramp." The twins developed a silent, synchronized lifting technique—Tyler on the back handles, Evan gripping the frame by the knees—to carry Ryan and his chair up fire escapes, loading docks, and stairwells.

To Evan, this wasn't a burden; it was the job. Just as the bass carries the melody, the bassist carries the singer.

Post-Apex Freedom

During the "Freedom Era" (post-1992), Evan's contributions became even more pronounced. His driving basslines on tracks like "Garbage" (from *The Warehouse Tapes*) and his ability to lock in with his brother's "Human Metronome" timing allowed the band to finally explore the raw, unpolished 80s rock sound that Apex Records had suppressed.

Wardrobe: This rejection of their old label defines his modern stage presence. After the 'Friction' scandal, Evan shed the polished 'Apex look' for good. On stage, he now proudly wears what he always has: jeans, sneakers, and a CPI Alumni t-shirt or hoodie, looking less like a rock star and more like the proud 'Forger' he is.

html:
The History

From the dorm rooms of CPI to the "American Dream" jackpot. The story of a family who fought the industry and won.

1985-1992: The Ironheads & The Cold War

The story begins at Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI) in Blacksburg. The five members (O'Connells and Wrights) formed a protective, insular unit—a "fortress"—to survive the academic and social pressures of the Class of '89.

Their early success attracted Apex Records, leading to a five-year "Cold War" over the band's identity. Apex wanted a pop band; The Stardust Engine wanted to be industrial rockers. This era was defined by "malicious compliance," hiding dark lyrics inside polished pop songs.

1992: The "Friction" Catastrophe

The Day The Contract Ended

In 1992, an Apex executive attempted to exploit the sibling bond between Ryan and Cassidy for a sexualized marketing campaign. The resulting confrontation—the "Dirty Mirror" incident—ended with Holly O'Connell (then a law student) forcing the label to void the contract.

The band was free, but they were blacklisted and broke. This marked the beginning of "The Wilderness Years."

1996: The "American Dream" Event

Daleville, VA (The Gas Station)

Late one night, returning from a gig in Lexington, the band stopped at a gas station in Daleville for snacks. Cassidy O'Connell bought a "Quick Pick" lottery ticket on a whim. She liked the visual pattern of the numbers.

The next morning, reading the newspaper over breakfast, she realized she had matched every single number for the American Dream Jackpot.

"She didn't scream. She just handed the ticket to Holly and said, 'Build us a fortress.'"

Jackpot Total: $2.04 Billion.

1997-Present: The "Loss Leader" Era

With the trust fund secured, the band ceased to be a commercial entity and became a "Loss Leader" for the family empire.

  • 1997: Released Hard Reset, their first album with an "infinite budget."
  • 2000: Founded Mirage (their own subsidiary label).
  • Today: They tour when they want, record what they want, and answer to no one.

title: Holly O'Connell | The Stardust Engine
description: Manager (CEO, Engine Room Records, LLC)
html:
Holly O'Connell

Manager (CEO, Engine Room Records, LLC)

  1. The Band
  2. Holly O'Connell

The "Anchor". Holly (Age 18 in 1987) is the most formidable member of The Stardust Engine, and she has never played a note on stage. An academic prodigy, she entered a Dual Enrollment program at age 16—attending Blacksburg High School in the mornings and riding Blue Ridge Transit Route 1 onto the Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI) campus every afternoon to take undergraduate business and commercial law courses alongside her older siblings and cousins.

While still dual-enrolled in high school and CPI, she took on the role of the band's manager at the Progress Street house. Her official role was to act as the emotional peacemaker—famously pulling Ryan and Cassidy into a "three-way hug" when they argued over music, reminding them "You're both right. And you're both idiots."

The First Redline: The 1986 CPI Mutual Cross-License

Holly's first legal masterstroke happened at the Progress Street kitchen table in October 1986, when she was a sixteen-year-old dual-enrolled high school junior taking afternoon undergraduate courses in Business Administration and Commercial Contract Law at CPI. When Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, and Tyler prepared to submit their cassette demo of "Ignition (The Forger's Call)" to the CPI Student Government Association's football anthem contest, Holly—with her CPI Commercial Contracts textbook open right next to her high school binder—read the fine print on the back of the entry form. Buried in Paragraph 4 was a standard boilerplate "Work Made for Hire" clause that would have permanently signed away 100% of the band's master and publishing rights to the CPI Athletic Foundation.

Refusing to let her family lose their song, Holly took a red pen to the entry form and marched into the Office of University Counsel. She negotiated a historic $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License: The Stardust Engine kept 100% of their master and publishing rights while granting CPI Athletics and the Marching Forgers a perpetual, royalty-free stadium and broadcast synchronization license to play "Ignition" (and future Stardust Engine stadium anthems) inside The Crucible. In exchange, CPI's Office of Trademarks & Licensing granted the band (and any label they wholly owned) a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free Co-Existence & Artistic Reference License to use the institutional marks CPI, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute, The Forgers, and The Crucible across their songs, album titles, and liner notes—a clause Holly pulled from the vault eighteen years later in October 2004 to stage the secret fourth-quarter stadium debut of "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible" forty-eight hours before Progress Street dropped.

The Crash of '90: "The Gatekeeper"

When Ryan was paralyzed in December 1990, Holly's role expanded from Business Manager to Medical Director. She holds Durable Power of Attorney for Ryan, giving her the legal authority to make medical decisions in an emergency. She carries signed, notarized HIPAA release forms in her briefcase at all times.

The "Friction" Nuke (1992)

Holly's true power was revealed during the 1992 "Friction" scandal. By this time, she was a 2L law student. When Julian Vance made his criminal demand, Holly transformed into "Holly the Shark". She secured the evidence that forced Apex Records to surrender the masters, using the freedom to found Engine Room Records, LLC.

CONFIDENTIAL: The "American Dream" Event (1996)

The Financial Architect

In 1996, when Cassidy handed her the winning lottery ticket worth $2.04 Billion, Holly didn't celebrate. She went to work.

"Money destroys families," she famously said. To prevent that, she spent the next two decades armoring herself with every credential available. She created the Forger Nation Trust, a structure that renders the band members "penniless" on paper—protecting them from lawsuits—while the Trust manages their empire.

title: Ryan O'Connell | The Stardust Engine
description: Lead Vocals, Lead Guitar
html:
Ryan O'Connell

Lead Vocals, Lead Guitar

  1. The Band
  2. Ryan O'Connell

As the oldest sibling (Age 23 in 1987), Ryan is the band's protective "Engine" and the voice of its raw rock energy. He famously delayed his own college entry so the entire "family" (his siblings and cousins) could enter CPI's Class of '89 together.

Archivist Note: Ryan hated the polish of the studio. He famously told producers that to find the real sound—the engine's hum—you couldn't float on the surface. You had to go Down. Deep Down.

The Crash of '90

The Live in Chicago (1990) album art captures the last time Ryan O'Connell stood on a stage. In December 1990, while driving back to Blacksburg on I-81 through a winter storm, Ryan was involved in a catastrophic black ice accident.

The crash resulted in a T10 spinal cord injury, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down. The "Stalemate Year" of 1991 wasn't just about fighting the label; it was about Ryan fighting to reclaim his identity. Apex Records pressured the band to hide his wheelchair or force him to sit on a high stool to "look normal." Ryan refused. He spent the year welding a custom, heavy-duty pedalboard and modifying his guitar rig to work from a seated position, proving the "Engine" was still running.

The "Freight Dog" Reality

Touring in the early 90s meant navigating a world built without him in mind. Venues rarely had ramps. Ryan often entered clubs through the loading dock, hauled up freight elevators alongside road cases and trash.

He relied on his cousins, Evan and Tyler, as his "Human Ramp." The twins developed a synchronized lift technique to carry him and his chair up fire escapes and narrow stairwells, ensuring he never missed a show. This gritty, unglamorous reality hardened the band's resolve and deepened their reliance on the "Family Unit."

The "Friction" Catastrophe (1992)

This context makes the 1992 "Friction" scandal even more harrowing. When executive Julian Vance demanded that Ryan and Cassidy perform a sexual act on camera, he was targeting a man who was less than two years into his life as a wheelchair user.

During the infamous "Dirty Mirror" incident, Ryan wiped the cocaine away not just because he was naive, but because he was sitting at eye-level with the table. To him, the white powder looked like falling drywall dust from the crumbling warehouse ceiling—just more filth he had to deal with. Vance's subsequent retaliation wasn't just professional malpractice; it was the exploitation of a disabled artist.

Ryan's roar of "SHE'S! MY! SISTER!" was the sound of a man reclaiming the power the industry had tried to strip from him. The resulting breach of contract left the band independent, but destitute, kicking off the four-year "Wilderness" period (1992-1996) where they survived solely on the loyalty of their fans.

His custom-built drum kit is a famous piece of rock lore, a massive 360-degree setup that dwarfs even the most extravagant kits of the prog-rock era. He is the source of the band's iconic, explosive, massive 80s gated reverb snare sound that defined their anthems. As Evan's twin, he shares a near-psychic connection with his brother, forming the tightest rhythm section in 80s rock.

Following his cousin Ryan's paralysis in 1990, the twins' role in the band went beyond music. in the early 90s, "accessibility" was a legal theory, not a reality. Venues often lacked ramps, elevators, or basic accommodations.

Tyler and Evan became Ryan's "Human Ramp." They developed a synchronized lifting technique to carry Ryan and his manual chair up fire escapes, loading docks, and narrow stairwells. While Holly and Cassidy handled the medical logistics, Tyler provided the brute strength required to physically move the tour. To this day, he is one of the few people Ryan trusts to lift him.

The "Ironhead" Connection

Tyler is arguably the most passionate "Ironhead" in the group. His ability to replicate the sound of a full marching band drumline was the key to the success of the "Forgers' Fight Song" on the *Live at The Crucible* album.

Ignition (The Forger's Call)

The most terrifying sound in college football.

The 1986 Contest

In 1986, long before they had a record deal, the five members of The Stardust Engine entered a student contest to replace the dated, traditional marching band song used for the CPI football team's field entrance.

They didn't write a fight song; they wrote a weapon. "Ignition" was designed as a heavy, industrial rock anthem meant to strike fear into opposing teams. It won by a landslide.

ARCHIVAL NOTE: This 2016 live album is the ONE and ONLY place you can find a commercially released recording of this track. Otherwise, you must physically attend a Saturday home game at The Crucible to hear it.

The Stomp

The Stomp was never part of the original 1986 sheet music. It started organically in the student section (specifically among the engineering students in the endzone) who began rhythmically stomping their feet on the concrete bleachers to keep time during the song's slow, building intro.

Over the decades, it blossomed into a terrifying 60,000-person synchronized ritual. Today, "The Stomp" is so loud and aggressive that it registers on the geology department's local seismographs. You cannot imagine the song without it.

DELIVERY DATE: JUNE 2002

The First Lift

The day the world opened up.

Delivery Bay 1

There was no red ribbon. There was no press. Just the humming of the factory lights and the smell of ozone and welding flux.

The "Iron Horse" (a custom Sainte-Claire 45H3) stood in the center of the bay—a massive forty-five-foot monolith finished in deep Obsidian Midnight lacquer and wrapped in sweeping Cosmic Nebula violet, cyan, and amber stardust graphics. The twenty welders and coachbuilders who had built it stood in a semi-circle, arms crossed, waiting.

Ryan O'Connell rolled onto the platform. The custom hydraulic system—over-engineered at Holly's insistence—hissed softly. He rose 60 inches into the air, the motion smooth and silent, and rolled into the main cabin.

He rolled back out onto the lift and lowered himself down. He looked at the foreman, a man named Jean-Paul.

"C'est parfait," Ryan said. "Merci, mes amis."

The applause from the crew was deafening. They weren't clapping for a client; they were clapping for one of their own.

ARCHIVE: 2002

The Sainte-Claire Protocol

The day the "Ironhead" reputation was forged in steel and perfect Québécois.

LOCATION: Executive Sales Office, Sainte-Claire Coachworks.
CONTEXT: The band is in the middle of their 2002 "Trans-Canada" Tour. They have just played three sold-out nights in Montréal, performing strictly in French.

Michel, the VP of Sales, rubbed his temples. He had just gotten off the phone with the manager of a major American Pop Star who was screaming in English about "Jacuzzi weight limits."

The door opened. Holly O'Connell (Age 33) walked in. She held the door open.

Ryan O'Connell (Age 31) rolled in past her. He maneuvered his manual chair with precision, turning to face the desk. He wasn't wearing sunglasses or a stage costume. He was wearing a flannel shirt and jeans.

Holly (in flawless Québécois): "Bonjour, Michel. Désolée du retard, le trafic sur la 20 était l'enfer."
(Hi Michel. Sorry I'm late, traffic on the 20 was hell.)

Michel blinked. He looked from the woman to the man in the wheelchair. "Madame O'Connell? Monsieur O'Connell? You... speak our language?"

Ryan (smiling, extending a hand): "On voulait pas vous forcer à parler anglais chez vous. C'est une question de respect."
(We didn't want to force you to speak English in your own home. It's a matter of respect.)

Holly sat down and slid a folder across the desk. It wasn't a rider full of demands. It was a structural engineering schematic for a heavy-duty hydraulic lift installation.

"I know you have a waitlist," Holly said (still in French). "I know the Pop Star wants a swimming pool. That is dead weight. This..." she gestured to her brother, "...is precious cargo."

"I don't need a party bus, Michel. I need a chassis that won't twist when I put a 400-pound industrial lift in the side door. I need steel."

The Outcome: Michel canceled the Pop Star's order that afternoon citing "irreconcilable engineering differences." He moved the O'Connell "Iron Horse" to Bay 1 immediately.
Flash Forward: 2018

When Holly returned 16 years later to commission Unit 01 (The Sovereign), the factory didn't ask for a deposit.

The floor crew remembered the American band that ate smoked meat with them in the breakroom and spoke their language. They started cutting the steel before the contract was even signed.

html:
Corporate Restructuring

The Delaware Migration

"We aren't hiding the money. We're hiding the targets."

August 12, 2015 // 21:00 EST // "The Bridge", Stardust Studios
The Architecture of Silence

The heavy blast door to "The Bridge" was locked. Inside, the massive tracking board that monitored the O'Connell Family Trust's global assets was glowing quietly.

Holly O'Connell stood at the head of the conference table. Spread out before her were five identical stacks of heavy, legal-weight paper, each marked with a different colored tab. She looked exhausted, but her eyes held the sharp, dangerous clarity of a predator that had just finished digging a very deep trench.

Ryan rolled his wheelchair up to the table, eyeing the stacks. Evan and Tyler took seats on the flanks, while Cassidy stood by the window, looking out into the dark industrial park.

"I passed," Holly said simply.

Cassidy turned, a massive smile breaking across her face. "The Delaware Bar? Holly, that's four states! You're a machine."

Evan offered a low whistle. "Virginia, New York, California, and now Delaware. Are you trying to collect them like trading cards?"

"I'm trying to build a moat," Holly replied, tapping the thickest stack of paper. "Virginia has been good to us. It's our home. But legally? It's too loud."

Ryan frowned, locking the brakes on his chair. "Loud how? We don't do press. We haven't done an interview in eight years."

"Paperwork is loud, Ry," Holly explained, leaning against the table. "Back in 1997 during Hard Reset—right after the '$13.99 War' and Cassidy's lottery win—I realized our money and our masters had to be siloed and diversified so a single lawsuit could never touch the family. While we were still recording and touring through Progress Street in 2004, I kept our core capital parked in Treasury ladders while running day-to-day music operations out of Engine Room Records, LLC. The moment we signed off the road after Last Bus Home in late 2004 to recover from burnout, I spent the next eleven years executing that 1997 blueprint—spinning off Stardust Strategic Assets, LLC for the hard equipment and coaches, Artists First Management, LLC for touring liability, and Stardust Properties, LLC and Pacific Rim Properties, LLC for real estate."

"Unbundling Engine Room Records into specialized LLCs between 2004 and 2015 kept our operations clean," Holly continued, "but right now, most of those entities are still registered in Virginia. If a reporter, or a rival executive, or a hostile litigator goes to the Virginia State Corporation Commission website and pays twenty dollars, they can see everything. They can pull the Articles of Organization. They see my name as the Registered Agent. They see our home address."

Holly pulled a marker out of her pocket and drew a large circle on the whiteboard.

"Right now, if someone pulls the thread on the indie band that lives in Blacksburg, that thread leads directly to a $2.4 billion commercial real estate portfolio. It leads to the student housing. It leads to Cassidy's lottery win. We are sitting ducks for a nuisance lawsuit."

Tyler crossed his arms, his biceps straining against his CPI t-shirt. "So, what does Delaware do?"

The Delaware Advantage

1. Absolute Anonymity: Delaware law does not require the names of the LLC members (owners) or managers to be disclosed on the formation documents. The only name on the public registry is the "Registered Agent."

2. The Court of Chancery: Corporate disputes in Delaware do not go to a jury trial where a slick lawyer can play on a jury's emotions. They go to the Court of Chancery—a court consisting solely of specialized corporate judges. Cases are resolved based on strict contract law, not theatrics.

"Delaware makes us ghosts," Holly said, answering Tyler's question. "If we move the entities to Delaware, the state doesn't ask who owns the company. They don't care. The only thing on the public record is the name of the Registered Agent."

"And usually," Holly continued, "billionaires hire third-party law firms to act as their Registered Agents. But third-party firms have paralegals, and paralegals gossip. They leak."

She tapped the Delaware Bar certificate resting on her desk.

"I didn't spend the last eight months studying corporate tax law just for the credential. I took the Bar so I can be the Registered Agent. Every single entity in our portfolio is going to be folded into a Delaware LLC, and I am the only lawyer with the keys."

The Execution

Holly handed out the heavy, black pens.

"We are dissolving the Virginia corporations tonight," she instructed, her voice dropping into its pure, unyielding 'Shark' register. "You are signing the Operating Agreements for the new Delaware entities."

She slid the first stack to Cassidy. "Artists First Management, LLC. This holds the touring contracts and the payroll. It's the shield that takes the hit if someone slips on a cable at a show."

She slid the next stack to Ryan. "Engine Room Records, LLC. This holds the master tapes and the copyrights. The vault."

Evan and Tyler received the real estate stacks. "Stardust Properties, LLC and Pacific Rim Properties, LLC. The cash engines. Completely firewalled from the music."

Finally, she placed a master document in the center of the table.

"And above it all, The O'Connell Family Revocable Trust. The sovereign entity that owns all the LLCs. No one outside this room will ever see this piece of paper."

Notary Protocol Executed

Because Holly obtained her Notary Public commission in 1994, no outside witnesses were required. The family signed the documents in absolute privacy. Holly stamped and sealed the formation of a $2.4 Billion empire without a single outsider knowing it happened.

Ryan signed his name with a fluid, practiced motion. He capped his pen and tossed it onto the table. He looked at his sister, realizing the sheer magnitude of the armor she had just bolted onto them.

"So," Ryan said, a slow, dangerous grin spreading across his face. "We're a multi-billion dollar conglomerate, but on paper, we're just an indie band from Virginia?"

"Exactly," Holly said, gathering the signed documents and walking toward the massive fireproof safe in the corner of the office. "If anyone tries to buy us, sue us, or exploit us, they're going to think they're dealing with five aging musicians."

She spun the dial on the safe, the heavy steel tumblers locking into place with a definitive, echoing CLACK.

"Let them think it. The iceberg is officially submerged."

The roar is gone. That's the first thing you notice. For 12 hours, the Aethelgard was a screaming metal tube fighting gravity. Now, it's a library.

The hardest part of space travel isn't the G-force. It's the clock.

To keep us from losing our minds in the eternal void, the Aethelgard runs a strict circadian simulation. At 0600, the panels blast us with blue-white light. At 2000, they shift to amber. "All hands, prepare for the Drop."

The ethereal synths of the Nebula are gone. The "Ship's Time" blue light is gone. The room is bathed in Emergency Red.

The Noise Floor

"The world did not sound like people said it did. It was made of frequencies."

01

High Fidelity

September 5, 1978 // Blacksburg High School

To Ryan O’Connell, the world was not made of words or conversations. It was made of frequencies.

Standing at the edge of the bus loop, clutching the strap of a canvas messenger bag that felt like sandpaper against his neck, Ryan cataloged the sonic landscape of his first day of high school. It was a war zone.

60 Hertz The aggressive hum of the streetlamp buzzing overhead, signaling a failing ballast.
1200 Hertz The squeal of the bus brakes, a high-pitched shriek that felt like a needle in his molars.
Low Freq Rumble The idling diesel engines, vibrating through the soles of his sneakers and up his shinbones.

He was fourteen years old. He was tall for his age, gangly, with hair that refused to lay flat. He looked normal enough, but inside, he was redlining.

"Ryan?"

His mother’s voice cut through the mix. She was leaning out of the window of their station wagon. She looked worried. She always looked worried when it came to him. In 1978, there wasn't a word for what Ryan was. There were only euphemisms: High-strung. Particular. Sensitive.

"You have your lunch?" she asked.

Ryan nodded. He couldn't speak. The transition from the safety of the car to the chaos of the sidewalk required all his processing power.

"Okay. Go get 'em, tiger."

He forced a smile—a mechanical lifting of the corners of his mouth that he had practiced in the mirror—and turned toward the building. Blacksburg High School loomed like a fortress of red brick and concrete. To anyone else, it was just a school. To Ryan, it was a sensory thresher.

He walked into the main hallway, and the volume spiked. It wasn't just auditory; it was physical. The air was thick with the smell of floor wax, cheap perfume, and locker room humidity. Hundreds of bodies collided, shouted, and slammed metal locker doors.

Clang. Slam. Laugh. Shout. Clang.

It was arrhythmic. Chaotic. There was no tempo.

Ryan kept his head down, counting his steps. One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. If he could impose a 4/4 time signature on the walk to his homeroom, he wouldn't drown.

He reached his locker—number 304. He dialed the combination. 12-24-36. Multiples of twelve. Good numbers. The locker opened with a satisfying metallic click. He placed his lunch inside and took a breath, pressing his forehead against the cool metal of the locker door. The metal vibrated slightly. Everything in the building was vibrating.

"Hey! Watch it, freak!"

Someone slammed into his shoulder. Ryan stumbled, his hip checking the locker frame hard. A senior in a varsity jacket pushed past him, laughing with a friend. Ryan didn't retaliate. He didn't even look up. He just felt the phantom impact on his shoulder, the lingering tactile burn.

The chaotic noise of the hallway surged—a wall of white noise that threatened to swallow him whole. He needed a filter. He needed an EQ pedal for reality.

He closed his eyes tight, right there in the middle of the hallway traffic. He imagined a mixing board in his mind. It was a trick he had taught himself over the summer.

INTERNAL MIXING CONSOLE
FADER 1: VOICES
STATUS: Slided down. Shouting becomes murmur.
FADER 2: LOCKERS
STATUS: Mids dipped. Metallic clanging loses bite.
FADER 3: THE HUM
STATUS: Boosted. HVAC fans targeted.

He focused on the ventilation system. The deep, steady drone of the massive HVAC fans on the roof. It was a constant B-flat. A steady, unwavering note.

Hmmmmmmmmmmmmmm.

Ryan latched onto that B-flat. It was safe. It was predictable. It was the anchor. He opened his eyes. The hallway was still chaotic, but the B-flat gave him a path to walk on.

He pulled a notebook out of his bag. It wasn't for schoolwork. The cover was drawn over in black marker with diagrams of star charts and guitar schematics he didn't fully understand yet. On the back cover, he had written two words in block letters.

PROJECT AETHELGARD

He didn't know what it meant yet. He just liked the sound of the words. They sounded like a place where the noise didn't hurt.

The bell rang—a harsh, dissonant electric buzzer that made Ryan flinch violently. The B-flat vanished. The chaos returned.

Ryan O’Connell took a deep breath, gripped his notebook like a shield, and walked into the noise floor of the ninth grade. He just had to survive four years.

He had no idea that the survival manual was waiting for him at home, in the hands of his eleven-year-old sister who had just discovered she could play a C-major scale on a toy keyboard.

02

Safe Harbor

September 5, 1978 // 3:45 PM // The O'Connell Driveway

The school bus—a rattled, yellow cage on wheels—screeched to a halt. To Ryan, the brakes didn't just squeal; they screamed at a frequency that felt like a drill bit boring directly into his molars.

He didn't say goodbye to anyone. He didn't look at the other kids. He gripped the strap of his canvas bag, kept his head down, and launched himself out of the folding doors the second they opened. He landed on the cracked pavement of his street. The bus pulled away, taking the cloud of diesel fumes and the roar of shouting teenagers with it.

System Telemetry:
  • > Heart rate: 110 BPM (Too fast).
  • > Shoulders: Tensed to the ears.
  • > Social Battery: Depleted.

To anyone else, the seven hours spent at school were just "education." To Ryan, they were wasted time. Every minute he spent in that building, navigating the chaotic noise and the confusing social cues, was a minute he wasn't with them. It felt inefficient. It felt like bleeding.

He turned toward the house. It was a modest suburban split-level, but to Ryan, it was a decompression chamber.

And on the front porch, sitting on the top step like two gargoyles guarding a cathedral, were his sisters.

Cassidy (11) was wearing oversized headphones plugged into nothing—just wearing them to muffle the wind. Holly (9) had a notebook on her lap and was organizing a pile of rocks she had found in the driveway by size and color.

Ryan let out a breath he felt like he’d been holding since homeroom. The mask dropped. The "High School Freshman" act—the stoic, silent, terrified performance—evaporated.

He didn't walk up the driveway. He ran.

"Ryan!" Holly shouted, abandoning her rock collection.

She hit him at full speed before he even reached the bottom step. She was small for nine, a dense little projectile of affection. She wrapped her arms around his waist, burying her face in his flannel shirt.

Ryan dropped his bag on the grass. He didn't pull away. He slumped into the hug. He wrapped his long, lanky arms around her, resting his chin on the top of her head.

Pressure. Squeeze. Grounding.

"Did you survive?" Holly asked, her voice muffled by his shirt.

"Barely," Ryan groaned. "The cafeteria smells like wet cardboard and shouting."

Cassidy stood up from the step. She didn't run; she drifted down to them. She slid under Ryan’s left arm, sandwiching him. She pressed her forehead against his shoulder, closing her eyes.

"You're vibrating," Cassidy noted softly. "Like a struck bell."

"Too much treble today," Ryan whispered, tightening the huddle.

He stood there on the front lawn, eyes closed, holding his sisters. This wasn't just affection; it was a recharge cycle. Without them, he felt like he would float away into the static. With them, he had gravity. Every second of school was just the price he paid to get back to this moment.

"Come on," Holly commanded, pulling back but keeping hold of his hand. "Mom's at the store. We have the perimeter."

"Perimeter secure?" Ryan asked, a small smile finally breaking through the exhaustion.

"Secure," Holly nodded seriously. "I made peanut butter toast. And Cass set up the station."

They walked inside, an entangled knot of limbs. Ryan didn't just walk through the door; he shed the armor. He kicked off his sneakers. He threw his bag into the corner.

They went straight to the living room floor. The carpet was shag, brown and orange—a tactile nightmare for some, but for Ryan, it was familiar ground.

Cassidy had dragged the family’s heavy console record player onto the floor. She had the sleeve of the biggest movie soundtrack of 1977 propped up against the sofa: "SOLARIS VANGUARD: Original Motion Picture Score" by Marek Solnik.

Ryan lay down on his back, staring at the textured ceiling. Cassidy lay down next to him, shoulder-to-shoulder, mimicking his posture. Holly flopped across both of their stomachs, acting as a weighted blanket.

"Side A, Track 1?" Cassidy asked.

"Please," Ryan said. "I need the Overture."

Cassidy dropped the needle.

The Solaris Overture blasted out. It began with a single, piercing trumpet blast, followed by the swell of a hundred strings. It was loud, but it was good loud. It was organized. It was heroic. It was math made into emotion.

Ryan felt Holly’s weight on his stomach, rising and falling with his breath. He felt the heat of Cassidy’s arm against his side.

"I hate ninth grade," Ryan said to the ceiling, the music washing over him.

"We know," Holly said, picking at a loose thread on his shirt. "But you're home now."

"Yeah," Ryan closed his eyes, his breathing finally syncing with the tempo of the orchestra. "I'm home."

For the next twenty minutes, nobody moved. They didn't speak. They just lay in the "Pile," listening to the fictional space opera, letting the frequency of the house reset their nervous systems. This was the prototype. Years later, when the world tried to crush them with contracts, lawsuits, and steering wheels, they would always return to this formation.

Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute

Blacksburg, Virginia //, Home of the Forgers & The Ironheads

The "Forger" Identity & The Ironheads

Nestled high in the Blue Ridge Mountains of Southwest Virginia, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI) is the Commonwealth's premier land-grant polytechnic research university. Its students, faculty, and alumni are known worldwide as "The Forgers"—a tribute to the institute's 19th-century origins in metallurgy, heavy foundry engineering, and industrial mechanics.

Inside The Crucible, CPI's 65,000-seat concrete-and-steel football stadium, that blue-collar identity is personified by The Ironheads. Just as Buchanan University basketball is famous ph and wide for The Pavilion Lunatics inside Buchanan Indoor Pavilion, CPI football is renowned across collegiate athletics for The Ironheads—the 20,000 fanatical students packed shoulder-to-shoulder onto the unpadded galvanized metal bleachers of the North End Zone (The Anvil). Wearing painted maroon-and-orange steel-mill hard hats and denim overalls, The Ironheads refuse to sit from kickoff to 0:00 and treat sideline decibel meters as a personal scoreboard.

Blacksburg & CPI Campus Gazetteer

Built from locally quarried grey-and-pink dolomitic limestone known universally as Ironstone, the CPI campus and the Town of Blacksburg operate as a living, interconnected grid where characters across eras and book series cross paths along the same quadrangles, halls, and transit corridors:

Commonwealth Green, Preston Hall, & Commonwealth Mall

Commonwealth Green is the vast central oval lawn at the heart of campus, ringed by neo-Gothic Ironstone academic halls and anchored on its northern rim by Preston Hall (the towering administrative headquarters housing the President's Office, Bursar, and 3,000-seat Preston Auditorium). Feeding the Green from the east is Commonwealth Mall, spanned by the iconic Ironstone arches of The Keystone Bridge (linking Keystone Hall to Pendleton Memorial Library). Before the dedicated multi-bay CPI Transit Center was constructed, every Blue Ridge Transit (BRT) route staged bumper-to-bumper along the curb of Commonwealth Mall beneath The Keystone Bridge in an infamous, diesel-choked nightmare—the exact curbside gauntlet where Erin rescued her twin brother John in November 2004.

Kincaid Hall, Callahan Hall, & The Engineering Quad

Along Commonwealth Mall sits Kincaid Hall (the bustling student union housing the Kincaid Ballroom, Kincaid Auditorium, and Second-Floor Lounge) and Callahan Hall (home to Services for Students with Disabilities / SSD). Directly northwest of Commonwealth Green rises the Engineering Quad—anchored by Faraday Hall (Electrical & Systems Engineering), Joule Hall (Mechanical & Materials Engineering), Kelvin Hall (Computer Science), and Archer Hall (General Lecture Hall)—while the Residential Quad is served by The Foundry, CPI's massive two-story rotunda dining hall.

Eleanor Bennett Commonwealth Hall ("The Old Lady") & Pepper Street

On campus, Eleanor Bennett Commonwealth Hall—known universally as Bennett Hall, "The Old Lady," or "The Old Lady on the Hill"—is a historic Ironstone residence hall whose Suite 214 serves as the sanctuary for Jordan Shawn Kelly, Aubrie, and the Group of 8 in The Aubrie Chronicles. Off campus, Progress Street NE is home to The Stardust Engine's Ironwood Collective, while the Pepper Street / Pepper Plaza corridor (anchored by Valu-Mart) houses Paige, Freddie, and Jessica at 105 Pepper Street.

The Crucible, The Furnace, & The I-81 Spine (Exits 118 & 98)

At the southern edge of campus stand The Crucible (65,000-seat football stadium) and The Furnace (10,000-seat basketball coliseum), both protected in perpetuity by the 1995 Ironhead Covenant. The university's reach extends down I-81 from the 8-level, 6,000-space Christiansburg Transit Center at Falling Branch (Exit 118) to the 566-acre New River Vocational Rehabilitation Center & Justin's Station (Exit 98) in Pulaski County.

The Class of '89 & Academic Precedents

CPI is the literal and spiritual birthplace of The Stardust Engine. All five members—Ryan O'Connell, Cassidy O'Connell, Holly O'Connell, Evan Wright, and Tyler Wright—walked across the stage together on The Commonwealth Green as proud graduates of the CPI Class of 1989.

1. The Dual-Enrollment Bridge (1985–1987)

When Ryan (21), Cassidy (19), and twins Evan and Tyler (18) matriculated as CPI freshmen in Fall 1985, youngest sister Holly O'Connell was only 16. Through CPI's joint High School Dual Enrollment partnership with Blacksburg High School, Holly attended morning high-school classes and rode Blue Ridge Transit Route 1 to the CPI campus every afternoon to take 200- and 300-level undergraduate Business Administration and Commercial Contract Law courses. By simultaneously satisfying her Virginia Advanced Studies Diploma and earning two full years of CPI credit, Holly entered CPI full-time as a Junior in Fall 1987 and graduated alongside her siblings and cousins in May 1989.

2. The Summer Session PolyPass Loophole

Under CPI regulations, a student's PolyPass (which turns a CPI student ID into a fare-free unlimited transit pass across Blue Ridge Transit and regional partners) does not normally activate for incoming freshmen until the Fall Semester begins in late August. However, savvy Blacksburg residents—like Jessica, Paige, and Freddie on Pepper Street—discovered that enrolling in a single accelerated Summer Session course (such as Session II: July–August) immediately activates the student's PolyPass upon tuition payment, unlocking two months of free summer mobility across the New River Valley.

The "Forger Nation War Chest" (1992–1995)

The unbreakable bond between CPI alumni and The Stardust Engine saved the band's career after the 1990 highway crash and the 1992 Friction catastrophe. When the family escaped Apex Records with their master tapes intact but their bank accounts drained, CPI students and alumni organized an underground, mail-order grassroots relief drive known as the "Forger Nation War Chest." Tens of thousands of five- and ten-dollar checks mailed in maroon-and-orange envelopes raised the seed capital Holly O'Connell used to incorporate Engine Room Records, LLC and record 1995's The Warehouse Tapes—forever linking the band's independence to the loyalty of Forger Nation.

Chapter 3 of 5 // Music & Contract Lore

Stadium Anthems & The 1986 Redline

"Ignition" (1986) //, The Stomp (1989) //, "Saturday Night Lights" (Oct 8, 2004)

1. The Birth of "Ignition (The Forger's Call)"

How a raw garage-metal cassette tape became the most terrifying pre-game entrance ritual in college football.

In October 1986, the O'Connell siblings and Wright twins (soon to be The Stardust Engine) entered a student-run contest to replace the traditional marching band fanfare that the CPI football team ran onto the field to. In their two-car garage on Progress Street NE, they recorded "Ignition (The Forger's Call)"—a heavy, pounding industrial-rock track anchored by drummer Tyler Wright striking a salvaged automobile brake drum with a sledgehammer (TING... BOOM!). On Saturday, October 18, 1986, the raw garage cassette made its thunderous pre-game debut over the PA system inside The Crucible—launching a Saturday night tradition that has shaken the Blacksburg valley ever since.

The 1986 Progress Street Redline: How a Dual-Enrolled 16-Year-Old Outsmarted University Counsel

When the CPI Student Government Association handed out the entry packet for the October 1986 anthem contest, the back of the standard release form contained a buried "Work Made for Hire" clause that would have transferred 100% of the winning song's master and publishing rights to the CPI Athletic Foundation. Sixteen-year-old prodigy Holly O'Connell—who was dual-enrolled at Blacksburg High School and CPI, riding Blue Ridge Transit Route 1 to campus every afternoon to take undergraduate business and contract law electives—refused to let her siblings and cousins sign it.

Sitting at the Progress Street kitchen table with a red pen days before the October 18, 1986 stadium debut, Holly struck the Work-for-Hire clause and negotiated a $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License with CPI's Office of University Counsel. Under Holly's agreement, The Stardust Engine retained 100% of their master and publishing rights while granting CPI Athletics and the Marching Forgers a perpetual, royalty-free synchronization license to blast "Ignition" (and future Stardust Engine anthems) inside The Crucible. In exchange, CPI's Office of Trademarks & Licensing granted the band (and any label they wholly owned) a perpetual, worldwide, royalty-free Co-Existence & Artistic Reference License to sing and print CPI, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute, The Forgers, and The Crucible in their songs and liner notes. Eighteen years later, in October 2004, Holly pulled that exact 1986 contract from the Engine Room Records vault to stage the most famous secret song premiere in college football history—and on October 18, 2011, the band celebrated the exact 25th Anniversary of "Ignition" debuting inside The Crucible by releasing their Burnout Hiatus retrospective, Starfield Calibration.

The 1989 Rivalry Game (Virginia Piedmont University) & "The Stomp"

What makes the tradition legendary is that its most terrifying element didn't exist when the band submitted their raw cassette in 1986. The rhythmic "Stomp" and the deafening crowd chants of "IGNITION!" evolved completely organically during a freezing November 1989 night game against traditional state rivals Virginia Piedmont University (VPU). Trying to stay warm and get rowdy, students packed into the North End Zone (The Anvil) started stomping their heavy winter boots on the galvanized metal bleachers in perfect time with Tyler’s recorded brake drum: TING... BOOM!

Because it was heavy boots on hollow steel bleachers, it echoed across the valley like cannon fire. During the pauses where Ryan screams "IGNITION!" on the tape, visiting VPU fans tried to boo—so 20,000 CPI students spontaneously roared "IGNITION!" right back at the PA system while mimicking the Marching Forgers' bridge cadence (swaying Left, Right, Left, Right in unison). By the mid-1990s, the Athletic Director cemented the ritual by cutting the stadium lights to pitch black right before the tape rolls, leaving opposing teams in the dark listening to 65,000 people register on the campus seismographs.

2. "BAH! BAH! BAH!": The Ironheads & The October 8, 2004 Secret Premiere

OCT 8, 2004 — 4TH QUARTER

How Holly O'Connell ambushed 65,000 fans during the Coal & Iron Border War against #6 Monongahela State—48 hours before Progress Street hit record stores.

Who Are "The Ironheads"?

Just as Buchanan University basketball is famous ph and wide for The Pavilion Lunatics inside Buchanan Indoor Pavilion, Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute football is known across the nation for The Ironheads—the diehard, fanatical student vanguard packed shoulder-to-shoulder onto the cold galvanized metal bleachers of the North End Zone (The Anvil).

Named in dual tribute to CPI's blue-collar metallurgy heritage and legendary benefactor Jeremiah "Ironhead" Vance (Class of '52), The Ironheads wear painted maroon-and-orange steel-mill hard hats and overalls, refuse to sit down from kickoff to the final whistle, and treat acoustic decibel meters on the sidelines as a personal scoreboard.

The Black Anvil Trophy ("The Coal & Iron War") OCT 8, 2004

The Stage: The Stardust Engine's homecoming album Progress Street was scheduled for release on Monday, October 10, 2004. Two nights earlier—on Saturday, October 8, 2004—CPI hosted fierce Appalachian border rival #6 Monongahela State University (MSU) inside The Crucible. Behind closed doors, Holly O'Connell had already executed a confidential addendum under her 1986 $1.00 Perpetual Mutual Cross-License with the CPI Athletic Director. Only three people in Blacksburg knew what was on the unmarked gold master CD-R hand-delivered to the press-box audio booth before kickoff.

As the clock hit 0:00 at the end of a bruising third quarter, CPI clung to a gritty fourth-quarter lead over #6 Monongahela State. Normally, the break between the third and fourth quarters belonged to the stadium organ or a standard marching fanfare. Instead, the press-box engineer faded the stadium lights to a deep twilight glow and pushed the master fader all the way up on Track 6 of Progress Street: "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible."

For the first four bars, 65,000 fans froze as Cassidy's triumphant 1980s analog synthesizer brass fanfare and Tyler's drumline cadence rolled across the valley. Then Ryan and Cassidy's voices echoed from the giant speaker arrays above The Anvil—singing directly about October '86, Progress Street, and "Sixty thousand standing in the maroon and orange sea / Waiting for the signal at CPI with me!"

When The Ironheads realized they were hearing a brand-new, unreleased Stardust Engine stadium anthem written specifically for them, The Crucible detonated. Just as Boston Beacons fans belt the eighth-inning horn hook of "Sweet Evangeline" at Back Bay Park, The Ironheads spontaneously locked onto Cassidy's three-note synthesizer brass fanfare at the end of every chorus line—roaring a deafening, stadium-shaking "BAH! BAH! BAH!" and chanting "SO GOOD! SO GOOD! SO GOOD!" between the verses. Riding the tidal wave of that fourth-quarter singalong, the Forgers defense stuffed Monongahela State's final drive to seal a 19–13 victory. By Monday morning, when Progress Street officially dropped on October 10th, the fourth-quarter "Saturday Night Lights" singalong was already cemented as an unbreakable CPI game-day tradition—turning "Ignition" into the pre-game war cry that starts the fire, and "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible" into the fourth-quarter victory celebration that seals it.

Chapter 4 of 5 // Transit & Infrastructure Lore

Falling Branch & The $150 Parking Paradox

I-81 Exit 118 //, 8 Levels & 6,000 Spaces //, Blue Ridge Transit Priority

1. The New River Valley Transit Grid & The PolyPass Ecosystem

In Blacksburg, Christiansburg, Radford, Carroll County, and the Roanoke Valley, public transit is not an afterthought—it is the circulatory system of the entire region. Anchored by Blue Ridge Transit (BT / BRT), the network is unified by the CPI PolyPass: every active CPI student and faculty ID card doubles as an unlimited, fare-free (`$0.00`) transit pass across four interconnected regional bus agencies (Blue Ridge Transit, Bluewater Transit, Roanoke Valley Transit, and Radford Transit).

Blue Ridge Transit's workhorse fleet consists of 29-foot, 35-foot, and 40-foot rigid coaches alongside 60-foot low-floor articulated transit buses manufactured by Prairie Coachworks, painted in the agency's signature "Mountain Mist & River Ribbon" livery (Arctic Fleet White upper bodies, Appalachian Pine Green lower skirts, and dual sweeping ribbons of New River Slate-Teal and Mountain Mist Sky Blue arcing across the black rubber center accordion bellows, with the flip-out aluminum ADA wheelchair ramp always deployed from the front passenger boarding door).

BT ROUTE 1 Every 15 Min (60' Artics)

The Spine (45 Min Full-Length)

Never short-turns: leaves Christiansburg Transit Center / Falling Branch (Exit 118), follows US-11 into downtown Christiansburg to Pepper Plaza Transit Center (next door to the Montgomery County Courthouse, across from 105 Pepper Street & Valu-Mart; 15 min), then follows South Main Street (Business US-460) and Progress Street NE into Blacksburg to Commonwealth Mall (2003–2015) or the CPI Transit Center (2016+; 30 min from Pepper Plaza).

BT ROUTES 2, 3, 4, 8 & 1X $1.00 / PolyPass $0 (1X: $0 All)

Christiansburg, "The Law School," & 1X

Route 2 (Cambria & Mall Local) runs 7 days/week from Pepper Plaza via Wades Ln (Stardust Blacksburg, LLC apartments), Mill Ln NE (Christiansburg Aquatic Center), and Cambria Station (800 Depot St NE) to NRV Mall Transit Center. Route 4 (Woodland Dr) interlines with Route 1 60' artics east along Roanoke St (Exit 118C hotels), deviates onto Simmons Rd NE to serve the CPI Christiansburg Campus (anchored by the CPI Schools of Law and Nursing plus main-campus overflow and evening classes, universally called "the Law School" by locals, students, and riders), and continues past Motor Mile to a VDOT 60' Turnaround Loop at Woodland Dr (every 30 min; boosted to every 15 min during the Fall 2014 & Fall 2019 hotel overflow crises alongside CPI Fleet Services shuttles; truncated at the Temporary VDOT Park & Ride at CPI Christiansburg Campus from 2010–Summer 2012 while Falling Branch was closed for construction, signed strictly 4 CPI CBURG). Route 1X (Crucible / Furnace Express) runs non-stop via the BUSES ONLY US-460 ramps and is 100% zero-fare for everybody (no PolyPass required). Route 3 links Pepper Plaza to Radford's McConnell Hub; Route 8 runs south on SR-8 to Riner.

BLUEWATER ("OTHER BT") $5 Express / $1 Local

The Maroon Express (90 Min)

Pulses from Bluewater Transit Center (across from Bluewater High School in Bluewater, VA—hometown of Madison Elizabeth Scott; local Purple Line serves Galax CC hourly). Hourly 45' coaches run via Exit 14 P&R, Max Meadows (Exit 84), Dublin / NRVRC Justin's Station (Exit 98), Falling Branch (Exit 118B), and New River Valley Mall (Christiansburg Mall) to CPI. Free with CPI PolyPass, Galax CC ID, or Carroll County Schools ID.

RVT EXPRESS & RAIL $3 Express / $2 Local

Roanoke Express & ARTS Thruway

Links downtown Roanoke's Campbell Court (earlier era) / Third Street Station (3rd Street Station) (later era, Mon–Sat) to Falling Branch, New River Valley Mall (Christiansburg Mall), and CPI—offset 30 minutes from Bluewater's Maroon Express for 30-minute combined express headways. On Oct 31, 2017, RVT launched the 7-day ARTS Train Connector meeting ARTS The Patriot trains in Roanoke with guaranteed delayed-train holds.

RADFORD TRANSIT 29' Buses • $0.50 → $0

McConnell Hub & School ID Rule

Operates 29-foot buses from McConnell Transit Center ($0.50 no-transfer fare pre-COVID; permanently 100% fare-free post-COVID). Free with CPI PolyPass, RU ID, Dublin CC ID, and Radford Public Schools ID (officially RHS only, though identical badge templates let middle and elementary kids ride free). Local routes (*Plumb Creek*, *Dublin CC*) run Mon–Fri; Radford Connector to CPI runs 7 days/week.

VALLEY FLYER NO POLYPASS ($15.99+)

D.C. Intercity Coach vs. 2003 MCI

State-sponsored intercity coach to Washington, D.C. Union Station (`$49.99` to D.C.; `$15.99` local hop between CPI and Falling Branch; skips New River Valley Mall & downtown Roanoke; no PolyPass or Go-Card accepted). Contrast with the 2003 Supplemental Commuter Coaches (45' MCI coaches running Falling Branch ↔ New River Valley Mall ↔ Commonwealth Mall every 30 min, free with PolyPass).

Chronological Evolution: From Flashing the PolyPass to the Blue Ridge Go-Card

ERA 1 // 2003–2015

Commonwealth Mall Curbside & "Flash Pass" Boarding

Prior to 2016, all five bus agencies converged curbside along Commonwealth Mall beneath The Keystone Bridge outside Kincaid Hall (headsign: 1 COMMONWEALTH MALL). There were no smart cards: CPI, Galax CC, Carroll County, RU, Dublin CC, and Radford students simply flashed their physical school ID cards to the bus operator at the front door.

ERA 2 // 2016 & OCT 31, 2017

CPI Transit Center & ARTS Roanoke Rail Extension

In 2016, the off-street multi-bay CPI Transit Center opened (`1 CPI TRANS CTR`), ending the Commonwealth Mall curbside bottleneck. On October 31, 2017, ARTS (American Rail Transit Service) extended its The Patriot train to Roanoke's Third Street Station, launching RVT's 7-day Train Connector Thruway service.

ERA 3 // POST-COVID (2020–2021+)

The Blue Ridge Go-Card, MagnaByte Express Mode, & POP

Following the COVID-19 pandemic, Blue Ridge Transit, Bluewater Transit, and RVT retired visual ID flashing and launched the contactless Blue Ridge Go-Card (while Radford Transit went permanently 100% fare-free). Embedded directly into new CPI PolyPasses, Galax CC IDs, and Carroll County IDs—and supporting MagnaPhone / MagnaWatch Express Transit Mode (tap without waking) and open-loop bank cards—the Go-Card automates daily/30-day fare capping, upgrade pricing, and GPS + Tap-Off zone billing on the northbound Maroon Express (charging `$1.00` for local Exit 14 hops vs. `$5.00` interstate). One year later, BT installed rear-door validators on 40'/60' buses for all-door Proof of Payment (POP) boarding.

ERA 4 // 2027 RAIL EXTENSION

ARTS Rail Reaches Christiansburg (Cambria Station)

Because existing Norfolk & Western / Virginian rail lines bypass Exit 118, ARTS restores the historic Cambria Station (800 Depot Street NE) in 2027 for The Patriot. Served all day by BT Route 2, select Route 1 60' artics (signed via CAMBRIA STA) deviate off N. Franklin St via Mill Lane NE (serving the Christiansburg Aquatic Center) and Depot St NE—using the grade-separated Franklin St bridge so 60' artics never cross the active rail tracks at grade.

2. The Christiansburg Transit Center at Falling Branch (Exit 118)

VDOT OWNED & OPERATED

Originally opened in 2003 as the surface-level VDOT Falling Branch Park & Ride (where buses and cars intermingled and exited via US-11) and rebuilt in August 2012 as the massive grade-separated Christiansburg Transit Center at Falling Branch (though locals in 2014–2016 still colloquially call it "Falling Branch" or the "Exit 118 Park & Ride"), the facility functions Monday–Friday as a regional commuter hub. On Forgers Football Saturdays and The Furnace arena nights, however, it reveals its true engineering purpose: a freeway intercept terminal where Blue Ridge Transit and CPI Fleet Services press every available bus into joint, fare-free Load and GO! service.

WSDOT-Style Asymmetric Freeway Geometry: Why the Bus Beats the Car

Inspired by Pacific Northwest transit-priority freeway interchanges, VDOT and CPI engineered the Christiansburg Transit Center with intentionally asymmetric highway ramps to answer a simple question: "Why should I park here at Exit 118 instead of driving another few miles into Blacksburg?"

  • Direct I-81 Ramps (All Vehicles): High-capacity flyover ramps lead directly from I-81 North and South straight into the 8-level, 6,000-space garage. Motorists exit the interstate and park without hitting a single surface traffic light—and after the game, discharge directly back onto I-81 North or South.
  • Direct US-460 Transit Flyover (BUSES ONLY): If a driver decides to keep driving toward Blacksburg, they cannot use the facility's direct high-speed connector. The grade-separated flyover ramp linking the ground-floor 8-bay BRT Terminal to the US-460 Bypass is strictly restricted to Blue Ridge Transit and regional partner coaches.
  • The Southgate Drive Golden Road: Where US-460 meets the CPI campus, Virginia State Police physically close Southgate Drive to private automobiles on game days—turning the entire arterial into an exclusive, signal-prioritized expressway for 60-foot BRT articulated shuttles straight to the gates of The Crucible.

Game-Day "Load and GO!" Operations

For a marquee Saturday night clash like the Coal & Iron War, VDOT overhead matrix signs on I-81 begin flashing CHRISTIANSBURG TRANSIT CENTER: GARAGE 82% FULL by mid-afternoon, and GARAGE FULL / USE ALTERNATE LOT hours before kickoff. Down on Level 1, the bus terminal operates completely separated from automobile circulation. Both Blue Ridge Transit 60-foot Prairie Coachworks artics and CPI Fleet Services buses stage across Bays 1–8 with their overhead amber LED signs flipping between CRUCIBLE SHUTTLE (or FURNACE SHUTTLE) and GO FORGERS! inbound, and CBURG TC SHUTTLE ↔ GO FORGERS! on the return trip (or FALLING BRANCH SHUTTLE ↔ GO FORGERS! during the 2003–July 2012 surface-lot era). It doesn't matter whether you board a BT or CPI bus: there are no fareboxes, no PolyPass taps, and no paper tickets—just Fare Free, Load and GO! As soon as ~100 fans crush-load an artic, the doors close, the dispatcher releases it onto the bus-only US-460 ramp, and the next 60-footer rolls immediately into the bay.

3. The Great CPI Parking Paradox ("The $150 Arrogance Tax")

POSTGAME EVACUATION PHYSICS

Every season, an arrogant visiting fan or first-time VIP scoffs at the idea of parking at Falling Branch—declaring "I'm not riding a bus with the riffraff; we're parking right by the stadium"—and happily pays $150 for a single-game pass beside The Crucible.

What that visitor fails to read is the fine print on the back of every CPI Athletics hangtag—a clause that CPI's Parking & Transportation office cheerfully points to when angry emails arrive on Monday morning:

Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute — Game-Day Parking Terms & Conditions

"Game-day parking fees reserve a vehicle parking space only. Parking location near The Crucible does not provide, guarantee, or imply priority departure from campus following athletic events."

In short: $150 buys a 500-yard walk to your car—and places your automobile at the exact geographic center of a 65,000-person pedestrian and vehicular bottleneck. When the game clock hits 0:00, the Commonwealth treats postgame traffic like an industrial evacuation grid:

1. The $150 Stadium Lot Trap

Mr. $150 reaches his luxury SUV in three minutes, starts the engine, and backs out—only to sit motionless for 90 minutes close enough to The Crucible to hear the empty bleachers being pressure-washed. Every intersection around the stadium is converted to outbound-only police control. When his GPS says "Turn left toward Southgate," a Virginia State Trooper points at a barricade and waves him north toward Prices Fork Road, where central campus lots are slowly metered into the outbound funnel.

2. The "South Main Street" Illusion

Inevitably, thousands of motorists think: "US-460 Bypass is going to be jammed; I'll outsmart everybody and take South Main Street (Business 460) through town to Christiansburg!" Unfortunately, 20,000 other motorists attended the same seminar on clever shortcuts. Unlike limited-access US-460, South Main Street is a municipal arterial with traffic signals, side streets, businesses, and pedestrian crosswalks—turning a "shortcut" into a bumper-to-bumper crawl.

3. The Falling Branch Advantage

Transit riders experience passenger queuing at the stadium barriers rather than vehicle gridlock. Four 60-foot artics and CPI Fleet Services buses pull up simultaneously (CBURG TC SHUTTLE / GO FORGERS!, or FALLING BRANCH SHUTTLE pre-August 2012), swallow 400 fans at a time, and are waved straight down bus-only Southgate Drive by State Troopers onto US-460 and the bus-only ramp into the Christiansburg Transit Center—moving 12,000+ people outside the Blacksburg traffic zone before turning them back into motorists right beside I-81.

Cross-Universe Narrative Connections: From Exit 98 to Progress Street

  • Amaya, Justin, & Meredith Hayes (Exit 98 / Justin's Station): Twenty miles south of Falling Branch at I-81 Exit 98 sits the 566-acre New River Vocational Rehabilitation Center and the cashless Justin's Station convenience store. When Justin Hayes and his 20-woman protective phalanx (The Wall of 20) board the 6:30 AM Bluewater Transit Maroon Express at Exit 98's sawtooth bays, they consume 21 of the 49 coach seats plus the ADA securement bay—creating a legendary morning bottleneck downstream at Falling Branch that forces late-arriving CPI students onto the 45-minute local Route 1 articulated buses.
  • Paige, Freddie, & Jessica (105 Pepper Street): Living along the Pepper Street corridor in Blacksburg, the trio utilizes CPI's Summer Session II enrollment loophole (`HPE 204`) to activate their PolyPass IDs two months ahead of the Fall semester, giving them fare-free access to BRT's air-conditioned low-floor buses all summer long.

Chapter 5 of 5 // Athletic Rivalries Archive

Blood Feuds of the Commonwealth

VPU (1989) //, #6 Monongahela State (2004) //, Virginia Dominion (2014–2015)

1. The Three Pillars of Forger Rivalry Lore

In the RaggieSoft universe, every autumn Saturday in Blacksburg is measured against three opponent institutions—each representing a distinct cultural, geographic, and historical clash with Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI):

THE OLD GUARD EST. 1895

Virginia Piedmont Univ. (VPU)

Charlottesville, VA // The Commonwealth Cup

Blue-collar Appalachian engineering versus Charlottesville patrician tradition. During a freezing November 1989 clash against VPU, students stomping heavy winter boots on The Anvil's steel bleachers birthed "The Stomp" and the deafening "IGNITION!" crowd chant.

BORDER WAR BLACK ANVIL

Monongahela State (MSU)

Morgantown, WV // The Coalminers

"The Coal & Iron War." A bruising Appalachian border blood feud. On Saturday, October 8, 2004, CPI upset #6 MSU (19–13) on the night "Saturday Night Lights: The Crucible" secretly premiered at the start of the 4th quarter.

THE BLOOD FEUD 2014 – 2015

Virginia Dominion (VDU)

Norfolk, VA // The Monarchs ("Norfolk")

"The Hammer vs. The Crown." Back-to-back Homecoming shutouts in 2014 (38–0 VDU) and 2015 (52–0 CPI) turned the upstart Monarchs from Hampton Roads into a personal blood feud that eclipsed the century-old VPU series.

2. The Hammer vs. The Crown: The 2014–2015 VDU Homecoming Shutout War

2014 – 2015 ARCHIVE

How back-to-back Homecoming shutouts turned Virginia Dominion University ("Norfolk") into the most combustible rivalry in Commonwealth sports history.

For decades, every CPI student and alumnus considered Virginia Piedmont University (VPU) to be the Forgers' undisputed arch-rival. That changed forever across twelve months in 2014 and 2015, when CPI scheduled a home-and-home non-conference series against Virginia Dominion University (VDU)—the upstart Monarchs out of Norfolk, Virginia. Because both schools weaponized their respective Homecoming Saturdays to stage the matchups—and both games ended in shocking, lopsided shutouts—the collision between the Blue Ridge Mountains ("Blacksburg") and Hampton Roads ("Norfolk") became an unforgettable chapter in CPI lore.

The Hubris: On Saturday, September 27, 2014, CPI hosted VDU inside The Crucible for the very first time. Ranked #3 in the nation with a Gridiron Trophy-candidate quarterback, CPI Athletics had scheduled unranked VDU as what everyone assumed would be effortless Homecoming "target practice." All week long, dorm doors across Bennett Hall and chalk murals on The Commonwealth Green depicted the CPI Forger's Hammer smashing the VDU Monarch's Crown under banners reading "BEAT NORFOLK!"

The Collapse: After CPI marched down the field on the opening drive only to push a chip-shot field goal wide left, VDU's unflashy, brute-force rushing attack systematically ground down the #3 Forgers. Eating the clock 4 and 5 yards at a time, VDU stunned the 65,000-strong crowd to lead 7–0 after the first quarter and 24–0 at halftime (after recovering a CPI fumble inside the final minute of the half). Thousands of stunned fans streamed for the exits as the Marching Forgers took the field, and VDU poured it on in the second half to seal a historic 38–0 shutout inside The Crucible.

Student groups in Norfolk printed thousands of commemorative "38–0" t-shirts, convinced they would humiliate CPI a second time in front of their own alumni.

The Receipts: CPI's players and coaching staff had spent 365 days staring at the 0–38 scoreboard stenciled onto every weight-room mirror in Blacksburg. Refusing to take their foot off the gas for sixty minutes, the Forgers walked into VDU's Homecoming party in Norfolk and delivered a merciless, retaliatory 52–0 shutout blowout—refusing to kick field goals, keeping their starting defense on the field until the final whistle to preserve the goose egg, and handing VDU an even larger Homecoming shutout humiliation on their own turf.

In RaggieSoft's literary canon (The Aubrie Chronicles), the September 27, 2014 Homecoming Humiliation (38–0) was the traumatic freshman-year game where Jordan Shawn Kelly—watching his new Blacksburg sanctuary get dismantled by the team from his abusive mother's Hampton Roads backyard—suffered a devastating halftime meltdown and fled back to Bennett Hall Suite 214 with the Group of 8. They were trying to beat the storm. Fresh off a show in Wytheville, the band was racing the weather reports to get back to Blacksburg before the highways closed.

Ryan was driving. He wouldn't let anyone else do it. He knew the trucks on I-81. He knew the "suicide lane" merges. He was doing everything right—40 MPH in the Holt Freighter, hazards on, white-knuckling the wheel while the rest of the family slept in the back.

It didn't matter. Another driver, impatient and inexperienced with the mountain pass, decided 40 was too slow. The impact was small, but on black ice, physics is unforgiving. The van didn't just slide; it tumbled.

Years later, Ryan would process the trauma of this night through his music. The critically acclaimed concept album Mile Marker 98 reimagines the violent highway crash as a tragic malfunction aboard a spacecraft drifting through the vast cosmos.

"He hates the chair. Absolutely loathes it.
But the girls begged for a walk. He's pushing through for them."

The New Reality: Protocol T-10

Ryan sustained a complete T10 spinal cord injury. He retained full use of his hands and "The Engine" (his upper body strength), but lost all function and sensation below the waist. The "Stalemate Year" of 1991 wasn't just a hiatus; it was a boot camp for survival.

The "Iron Dome" (Morning Routine)

Spontaneity died on I-81. Ryan requires 60 minutes every morning for a strict Bowel Program. Because his body can no longer regulate this automatically, it must be manually triggered on a strict schedule to prevent accidents.

Holly's Role: She enforces the "Iron Dome." No interviews, no load-ins, no visitors before 10:00 AM. The tour bus does not move during this hour.

The 4-Hour Clock (Hydration)

Ryan manages his bladder via Intermittent Catheterization (IC) every 4 hours. If he waits too long, he risks kidney damage or Autonomic Dysreflexia (a life-threatening blood pressure spike).

The Logic: He constantly calculates water intake vs. showtime. On the 1990s tour buses, this meant relying on discreet urinals in his bunk, often assisted by Cassidy or Holly when his hands were too tired from playing.

The Pressure Clock

If Ryan sits still for >2 hours, skin tissue dies (pressure sores). He must perform a "weight shift" (lifting himself off the seat) every 15 minutes.

Cassidy's Role: She is his "Spotter." During interviews or studio sessions, she watches the clock. A subtle tap on his shoulder is their code: "Lift." She also handles the nightly skin checks, looking for red spots that Ryan cannot feel or see.

The "Freight Dog" Reality

The ADA passed in 1990, but venues in 1991 didn't care. Stages were inaccessible. Ryan often entered venues through loading docks and freight elevators, hauled up alongside the gear.

The Twins' Role: Evan and Tyler developed a synchronized two-man lift to carry Ryan and his chair up fire escapes and narrow stairwells. They became his legs.

August 15, 1995 //, 65,000 Stadium & 10,000 Coliseum //, "The Loudest House in College Sports"

Engineering a Seismic Complex: The Crucible & The Furnace

Sportscasters and visiting coaches across the nation refer to The Crucible (CPI's 65,000-seat football stadium) and its adjacent 10,000-seat vaulted concrete basketball arena, The Furnace, as "The Loudest Complex in All of College Sports"—and that reputation is not hyperbole. It is the result of deliberate, uncompromising acoustic and structural engineering tucked into a natural mountain amphitheater in Blacksburg, Virginia.

1. Vertical Bowl & Vault Geometry

Unlike sprawling, shallow suburban stadiums that allow crowd noise to dissipate into the sky, The Crucible's towering concrete East and West stands rise at an aggressive vertical pitch directly over the sidelines, while next door The Furnace traps basketball crowd noise beneath a steeply raked, low-slung parabolic concrete barrel vault.

2. "The Anvil" (North End Zone)

The Crucible's North End Zone—known universally as The Anvil—is constructed of unpadded, hollow-underneath galvanized steel bleachers housing 20,000 standing students (The Ironheads). When 40,000 winter boots strike those steel planks in unison, the bleachers act as a massive mechanical drumhead.

3. Zero Luxury-Suite Dampening

When rival universities tore out lower-bowl student seating in the 1990s to install sound-absorbing glass luxury boxes and carpeted club lounges, CPI was legally forbidden from doing so in both The Crucible and The Furnace by the 1995 Ironhead Covenant—preserving raw concrete, exposed structural steel, and maximum decibel retention.

THIS AGREEMENT is made and entered into this 15th day of August, 1995, by and between JEREMIAH "IRONHEAD" VANCE (hereinafter referred to as the "Donor") and THE BOARD OF VISITORS OF COMMONWEALTH POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE (hereinafter referred to as the "University").

ARTICLE II: THE COVENANT (THE "IRONCLAD CLAUSE")

Acceptance of the funds described in Article I is strictly conditional upon the University’s perpetual adherence to the following restrictions regarding the outdoor football stadium currently known as "The Crucible" AND the adjacent indoor basketball and convocation coliseum currently known as "The Furnace" (hereinafter collectively referred to as "The Protected Facilities"). These conditions run with the land and apply to the current structures and any future structures built to replace them.

Section 2.1: Naming Rights in Perpetuity

The names of The Protected Facilities shall remain, in perpetuity, "THE CRUCIBLE" (for the football stadium) and "THE FURNACE" (for the basketball and convocation coliseum).

  • (a) No corporate, commercial, or individual name shall ever be appended, prefixed, or hyphenated with either name (e.g., "The Crucible at [Corporate Name]" or "[Corporate Name] Arena at The Furnace" is expressly prohibited).
  • (b) The University agrees that The Crucible and The Furnace are places of metallurgical transformation and competitive fire, not corporate billboards. The integrity of both names is absolute.

The Donor asserts that the defining characteristic of The Protected Facilities is their sonic hostility to opposing teams. Therefore:

  • (b) The architecture must "serve the roar." Verticality, vaulted concrete reflection, and noise-trapping engineering must take precedence over aesthetics or luxury seating.

Section 2.3: The Spirit of Iron

  • (a) The primary visual materials of both structures shall remain concrete and steel.
  • (b) In The Crucible, the "North End Zone" (The Anvil) shall remain general admission bleacher seating to foster the intensity of the student section. In The Furnace, lower-bowl courtside risers shall remain student-priority seating. Comfort shall never supersede volume.
ARTICLE III: THE CLAWBACK PROVISION (PENALTY FOR BREACH)

The University acknowledges that this Gift is a binding contract, not a suggestion.

In the event that the University, its Board, or its Athletic Department violates any provision of Article II (specifically the renaming of either The Crucible or The Furnace, or the destruction of their acoustic character):

  2. The Penalty: The University shall be liable to repay the principal PLUS Compound Interest calculated at the Federal Prime Rate plus two percent (2%), accruing from the date of this Agreement (August 15, 1995) to the date of the breach.

Jeremiah "Ironhead" Vance, Donor
